name: Baker Aloe
notes: A small, clumping aloe from Madagascar with speckled, toothed leaves and orange-red tubular flowers. Soak, then let the soil dry out completely. Keep it under shelter from heavy monsoon rain. Aloes are toxic to cats and dogs.

name: Burle Marx Philodendron
notes: A compact, spreading philodendron with glossy, heart-to-arrow-shaped leaves, named after landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx. Water when the top 3–5 cm is dry. Thrives in Singapore's humidity; give it a short pole or let it trail. Toxic to pets.
soil: Chunky aroid mix with bark and perlite

name: Common Asparagus Fern
notes: Not a true fern but a feathery climbing asparagus. Keep the soil evenly moist and give bright, filtered light; yellowing fronds mean too much sun or drying out. The berries are toxic to pets.

name: Desert Rose
notes: Its swollen base (caudex) stores water, so let the soil dry between waterings and keep it out of prolonged rain, which rots the stem. Needs full sun to flower well. The sap is highly toxic to people and pets; wash hands after pruning.
soil: Very free-draining gritty mix, shallow pot

name: Everfresh
notes: A popular Singapore houseplant whose fine leaflets fold up at night and open again in the morning. Keep the soil evenly moist; dry soil makes it drop leaves. Give bright indirect light or gentle morning sun. Toxicity to pets is not well documented, so keep it out of reach.

name: Golden Pothos
notes: Known locally as money plant. Let the top half of the soil dry; drooping leaves mean it's thirsty. Also grows in plain water; change the water weekly so mosquitoes can't breed. Toxic to pets.
soil: Standard potting mix with perlite, or a jar of water

name: Indian Laurel
notes: A tough, fast-growing fig used for hedges, topiary and bonsai. Keep the soil evenly moist in full sun; leaves drop if it dries out or is moved suddenly. The milky sap can irritate skin and is toxic to pets.

name: Japanese Garden Juniper
notes: A low, spreading conifer often grown as bonsai. Needs full sun and good airflow. Singapore's humidity makes it prone to fungal problems, so water the soil, not the foliage, and let the surface dry slightly between waterings. Mildly toxic to pets.

fertilizer: Citrus fertilizer with magnesium and iron
name: Lemon
notes: Potted citrus in full sun usually needs water daily or every other day in Singapore's heat; skip after heavy rain. Yellow leaves can mean waterlogging or a nutrient shortage. Not listed as toxic to pets, though the peel oils can upset cats and dogs.
soil: Well-draining potting mix, large pot with drainage holes

name: Moss Rose
notes: A low, spreading succulent with fleshy needle-like leaves and bright cup-shaped flowers that open in full sun and close by late afternoon or on overcast days. Let the top of the soil dry between waterings; it tolerates drought but sulks in waterlogged soil after heavy rain. Pinch back leggy stems to keep it full. Toxic to cats and dogs.
soil: Sandy, free-draining mix, shallow pot or hanging basket

name: Mottled Spurge
notes: A columnar succulent euphorbia with marbled green-and-white ridged stems. Water only when the soil is fully dry and keep it sheltered from heavy rain. The milky sap is very irritating to skin and eyes and toxic to pets; wear gloves when handling.

fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer at half strength; a low-nitrogen bloom feed as buds form
name: Queen of the Night
notes: A night-blooming epiphytic cactus: its large white flowers open after dark and fade by morning. Let the top few cm dry between waterings, as it rots if waterlogged. Give bright, dappled light; hot afternoon sun scorches the flat stems. Generally considered non-toxic to pets.
soil: Chunky, fast-draining mix of orchid bark and perlite

name: Satin Pothos
notes: Matte, velvety leaves splashed with silver; leaves curl inward when it needs water. Let the top half of the soil dry between waterings. Toxic to pets.
soil: Airy aroid mix with bark and perlite

name: Silver Inch Plant
notes: A trailing plant with silver-striped purple leaves; the colour is strongest in bright indirect light. Keep the soil lightly moist and pinch the tips to keep it bushy. Its sap can irritate skin and it is mildly toxic to pets.

name: Snake Plant
notes: Let the soil dry out completely. In an air-conditioned room it may need water only every 2–3 weeks. Overwatering causes root rot. Toxic to pets.
